title: Fire from Between the Cherubim
summary: Ezekiel sees a sapphire throne above the cherubim. The man clothed in linen is told to take burning coals from among the wheels and scatter them over Jerusalem. The glory of the LORD rises from the cherubim to the threshold of the temple, filling the court with brightness, and then moves to rest above the cherubim, who carry it to the entrance of the east gate. Ezekiel realizes that these cherubim are the living creatures he first saw by the River Kebar.
story: This is the third scene in the temple vision of chapters 8 to 11. Chapter 8 exposed the idolatry in the temple, and chapter 9 showed the city's guilty inhabitants struck down while the faithful were marked. Chapter 10 now shows fire falling on the city and the glory of God preparing to leave. In 9:3 the glory had moved from the inner sanctuary to the threshold; here it moves from the threshold to the waiting cherubim (verse 18), and they carry it to the east gate (verse 19). One more step remains, in chapter 11. The chapter also links the end of Ezekiel's temple vision to its beginning in chapter 1: the same throne-chariot that met him in exile is the one now leaving Jerusalem.
historical:
The vision belongs to the date given in 8:1, about 592 BC, some six years before the Babylonians burned the temple in 587 or 586 BC. The burning coals scattered over the city anticipate that event: 2 Kings 25:9 records that the Babylonian commander Nebuzaradan burned the house of the LORD, the king's palace, and every great house in Jerusalem.

For the exiles who heard Ezekiel's report, the chapter answered a question that must have haunted them. Could God's presence be anywhere other than the temple in Jerusalem? Ezekiel had already seen the glory of God by a canal in Babylon (chapter 1). Now he learns that the same glory is leaving Jerusalem. The throne of God is mobile. It is not bound to a building or a land, and it is not held hostage by a city that has abandoned him.
cultural:
Cherubim were winged guardian figures well known in the ancient Near East. Composite winged creatures, often with human heads and animal bodies, guarded palaces and temples in Assyria and Babylon, and the exiles would have seen such figures in Mesopotamia. In Israel's worship, two golden cherubim stood on the lid of the ark of the covenant, and God was described as enthroned between or above them (1 Samuel 4:4; Psalm 80:1). Solomon's temple had two great carved cherubim in the inner sanctuary (1 Kings 6:23-28). Ezekiel's vision shows the reality those images represented: living beings who bear the throne of God.

There is one change from chapter 1. There, each creature's four faces were those of a man, a lion, an ox, and an eagle (1:10). Here the ox is replaced by the face “of a cherub” (verse 14). Interpreters have offered several explanations, including that the ox face was the one most characteristic of a cherub, or that the text reflects variation in how the vision was recorded. The difference is noticeable but does not affect the chapter's meaning.
literary: Chapter 10 is closely tied to chapter 1, and it reads as a deliberate recapitulation. Ezekiel repeats the details of the wheels, the eyes, the four faces, and the wings, and then twice states his recognition: these were the living creatures he had seen by the River Kebar (verses 15, 20). The chapter's action is simple (coals taken, glory moves, cherubim rise) but it is slowed by description, so that the reader lingers over the throne as it prepares to depart. The main line of movement is marked by the glory's positions: over the threshold (verse 4), above the cherubim (verse 18), and at the east gate (verse 19). Verse 8 is a parenthesis, an aside in the middle of the action.

outline.t: A sapphire throne, and coals for the city
The glory rises to the threshold and fills the court
A cherub hands fire to the man in linen
The wheels and the cherubim described
The glory moves to the east gate, and the prophet recognizes the living creatures

doctrines.note: The glory of God fills the court with brightness even as it prepares to leave. God's holiness is not diminished by his people's sin, but it will not remain where it is dishonored. His departure is itself a judgment.

The throne above the cherubim is a throne of rule. The same fire that is God's presence becomes the fire of judgment on the city, and it is handed out only at his command. Jerusalem's fall is not a defeat of God but an act of his government.

The mobile throne shows that God is not confined to a place. He met Ezekiel in Babylon, and he can leave Jerusalem. This was a hard truth for those who trusted the temple, and a hopeful one for the exiles.

words.note: Keruv, cherub (plural cherubim). The word appears twenty-one times in this chapter alone. Cherubim guard the way to the tree of life in Genesis 3:24, overshadow the ark, and are carved throughout the temple. Here they bear the throne of God. Popular art made cherubs into chubby infants; the biblical cherubim are powerful and awe-inspiring.

Ophan, wheel. The wheels beside the cherubim, gleaming like beryl and full of eyes, show a throne that moves in every direction without turning (verse 11). Later Jewish tradition treated the wheels, the ophanim, as a class of heavenly beings, but in Ezekiel they are part of the throne-chariot.

Galgal, whirling wheel. Ezekiel hears the wheels called by this name (verse 13). It is a different word from ophan and suggests rolling or whirling motion, perhaps like a whirlwind. The throne is alive with movement.
Kavod, glory. It appears four times in this chapter, marking each stage of its departure. The glory that once filled Solomon's temple at its dedication (1 Kings 8:10-11) is now leaving it.

christ: The glory that leaves the temple in Ezekiel's vision is the glory that the New Testament says came to dwell in Jesus. John writes that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us and that we saw his glory (John 1:14), and Paul speaks of the glory of God in the face of Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). The burning coals taken from beside the throne may also recall Isaiah 6, where a coal from the altar touched the prophet's lips to take away his guilt. In Ezekiel the fire judges; in Isaiah it cleanses. The New Testament holds both together at the cross, where judgment and cleansing meet. These links are thematic, not predictions within the text.
questions: Ezekiel recognized that the throne leaving Jerusalem was the same one that met him in exile. Where have you found God present in a place you did not expect?
The people trusted the temple as a guarantee of God's presence. What visible things do you rely on as proof that God is with you?
The same fire is God's presence and God's judgment. How do you hold together God's nearness and his holiness?
